prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realisation of the optical lattice clock, which made possible atomic frequency standards with fractional uncertainty near 1e-18

statement.case_for: I keep optical lattice clocks first. The central idea is specific and checkable: Katori's magic-wavelength lattice cancels the light shift on the clock transition, so many atoms can be interrogated at once while Doppler and recoil effects are suppressed. Ye's strontium work then showed that this approach reaches stability and accuracy near 1e-18. This rests on atomic structure I can judge from my own field: dynamic polarizabilities, blackbody-radiation shifts, higher-order lattice shifts and clock-transition properties. Independent confirmation across many laboratories and species, including direct clock comparisons, is as strong as for any candidate on the shortlist. The practical consequences are concrete: tests of fundamental constants and of time dilation on millimetre scales, relativistic geodesy, and the formal route to redefining the second. The credit is also unusually clean: Katori for the concept and first demonstration, Ye for taking it to the limiting performance. That gives a two-person prize without forced exclusions among the credited names.
statement.case_against: The strongest objection is that precision timekeeping has already been honoured twice recently, with frequency combs in 2005 and trapped-ion control in 2012, so a committee could see lattice clocks as an incremental extension of a recognised lineage. The fundamental-physics results so far are null tests rather than discoveries, and the redefinition of the second has not happened. I also have to admit a bias: this is the subfield where my technical judgement is strongest, and that may lead me to rate it above candidates I cannot assess in the same detail. Other lattice-clock contributors such as Lemonde and Ludlow are outside the credited names, so the credit is clean only on the supplied record. Finally, B009 has much broader opening support than any other candidate, and I cannot dismiss that.

responses.point: Danielsson ranks magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene first as a clear discovery with a theoretical prediction behind it, and ranks optical lattice clocks second as mature and thoroughly confirmed, with possible overlap with the 2005 and 2012 prizes.
responses.response: I agree that the Bistritzer-MacDonald prediction followed by the 2018 observation is a very clean narrative, and it is why I keep B009 as an alternative. Where I differ is on the weight given to the unresolved pairing mechanism. You treat it as compatible with good timing. I put it third mainly because the interpretation of the superconductivity is still moving, whereas for lattice clocks the physical mechanism and the error budget are understood and checked in many laboratories. On your point about overlap with earlier prizes, I think the distinction is real: combs supplied the frequency ruler and ion clocks supplied single-particle control, but the many-atom magic-wavelength scheme is a separate concept with its own physics.

responses.point: Kroll ranks lattice clocks first, arguing that Katori and Ye are the natural pair and that independent confirmation is strong, while noting the question of distinctness from the 2005 comb and 2012 ion prizes.
responses.response: I agree with your attribution and maturity reading, and I share the concern about distinctness from earlier prizes. I would qualify one point: your caveat that Hall and Hansch's comb work is already recognised should not push us to cite the clock as merely an application of combs. A citation that says the magic-wavelength lattice made the many-atom clock possible keeps the prize on the new idea. I also take your note that PTB, NIST and SYRTE confirmations are important for maturity, but they do not undermine the pair, since the concept and the leading demonstrations are what the credit is based on.

responses.point: Johansson ranks lattice clocks seventh, granting that precision metrology has a strong Nobel tradition and that the technology is mature, but stressing that fundamental-physics results so far are null tests and that Lemonde, Ludlow and others could claim credit.
responses.response: The null-test point is fair, and it is a real reservation. I would answer that the prize tradition for measurement does not require a new particle or effect, and the 2005 and 2012 citations rewarded methods that opened a new regime of precision. The 1e-18 level already gives measurable gravitational redshift across a millimetre-scale sample, which is a physical observation rather than a null result. On credit, I accept Lemonde and Ludlow contributed to the early programme, but the concept and first realisation are Katori's and the limiting performance is Ye's. You also rank circuit QED first, and I do see its quality, but its closeness to the 2025 prize on macroscopic quantum tunnelling in circuits makes me prefer to wait, a concern you share in your own uncertainties.

responses.point: Mehlig places lattice clocks eighth, finding the invention clear and of lasting metrological impact but noting that the redefinition of the second has not happened, so recognition could be timely or slightly early, and flagging overlap with the comb and ion prizes.
responses.response: I would resist the idea that the prize should wait for the redefinition of the second. The scientific achievement is already complete: the 1e-18 uncertainty has been demonstrated and verified by comparisons, and the redefinition is a metrological decision that follows from it rather than a test of it. Waiting would reward administrative timing instead of the discovery. I do share your concern about overlap with earlier precision prizes, and I would not defend the candidate on application alone. Your own top choice, active-matter hydrodynamics, is intellectually attractive, but I cannot judge it well and I note that it received only one ranking, so I cannot see a path to a broad committee view on it.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks twisted bilayer graphene first on the strength of the unusually clean theory-to-experiment chain and the three-person credit, while acknowledging that other moire band theory contributors are not credited and that the superconductivity origin is debated.
responses.response: I agree the theory-plus-experiment structure is a real strength and the three credited names are a natural set. My reservation is attribution at the edges: Lopes dos Santos, Peres and Castro Neto did earlier moire flat-band work, and Cao, Dean and others carried the experiments, which you also acknowledge. That makes the claim somewhat less closed than for the two-name lattice-clock credit. I would not oppose B009 as a laureate choice, and if the committee prefers it I would support the three-person form, but I think its interpretive uncertainty and relative youth give lattice clocks the safer case for this year.

uncertainties: Whether the committee regards lattice clocks as sufficiently distinct from the 2005 frequency-comb and 2012 ion-control prizes.
Whether other early lattice-clock contributors such as Lemonde and Ludlow have a claim strong enough to change the two-person credit.
Whether B009's broader opening support should outweigh its relative youth and the unsettled superconducting mechanism.
How far my specialist confidence in the atomic-physics details is influencing my ranking relative to candidates I know less well.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent for B049, B009 or B012 from my profile. My documented collaborators and contacts (the Gothenburg group of Lindgren, L'Huillier and Lund colleagues, Keller's group at ETH, Schuch, Dahlstrom, Argenti, Indelicato) are not among the credited names for these candidates. I am an atomic physicist working on theory close to the optical-clock field, which is a disciplinary closeness, not a personal tie, and I note it as a possible bias in my own uncertainties.
